Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

phwstyle (development version)

This release makes every function check what it is given. Where a call used to draw a wrong chart, drop content without a word or fail inside another package, it now does the right thing or stops with a message that says what to change.

Changes that may affect existing code

  • phw_add_slide() and a slide deck made with R Markdown stop with a message for a table with bars from phw_flextable_bars(). PowerPoint tables cannot show pictures, and before, the slide showed the numbers without the bars and gave no warning.
  • phw_plotly() stops with a message for a patchwork, such as a figure from phw_arrange() or g1 + g2, and shows how to combine the charts with phw_plotly(plotly::subplot(g1, g2)), which gives a group the same colour in every panel. Before, it drew only the last chart and dropped the others, the figure title and the source without a word.
  • The default palette "main" now has six colours: navy, teal, orange, pink, green and gold. Charts with five or six groups change colour, and charts with more than six carry on into "extended" after the sixth. "extended" is now "main" followed by wine, mint, bright green, blue, dark orange and black. Black comes last, so it no longer appears in a chart with five groups, where it read like a total. The three colours that were not PHW colours (#5A82E6, #274309, #730BB1) are gone. "accessible" has the same eight colours, with black and the dark rose-brown moved to the end. Gold is below 3:1 contrast on white, so it suits bars and areas better than thin lines. A saved colour key keeps the colours it already gave its groups.
  • Text dates must be ISO dates such as "2026-11-14". phw_epicurve(), phw_date() and the caption date stop on text such as "05/01/2026" instead of misreading it, and show how to convert it. phw_epicurve() also stops on a numeric date column. A blank text date, as read.csv() reads an empty cell, counts as a missing date.
  • A blank text group, as read.csv() reads an empty cell, counts as a missing value in phw_epicurve(), phw_pyramid(), phw_crosstab(), phw_group_table() and phw_summary_table(). It shows as “Unknown” (or the missing label), or is left out with a message when missing = NULL. Before, it became a group of its own with no name, which stopped phw_epicurve() when printed and gave tables a made-up column heading.
  • Rows with a missing date, count, value, estimate or code are left out with one message saying how many. Before, they could turn a whole period into 0 or blank a chart. phw_crosstab(missing = NULL) and phw_group_table(missing = NULL) now also say how many rows they leave out for a missing row or column value. phw_rate_table() and phw_risk_table() handle missing values as before.
  • phw_reactable() rows are no longer striped by default, to match the other tables. Pass striped = TRUE to stripe them.
  • Tables on PowerPoint slides stay readable when projected. Text in a table is never smaller than 12 pt, in a deck made with phw_add_slide(), R Markdown or the Quarto phw-pptx format, so phw_flextable()’s 10 pt text shows at 12 pt there. A table too long for the slide tightens its row spacing, and if it still does not fit, its rows continue on further slides. Each slide repeats the header row and the caption, marked “(continued)”, and the source goes on the last slide. A group or variable heading stays on the same slide as its first row. The source line phw_add_slide() puts at the bottom of a slide is 12 pt too. Set your own wording with the new continued argument of phw_flextable() and phw_add_slide(), for example for Welsh. Before, rows past the bottom of the slide were lost: a knitted deck dropped them without a warning, and phw_add_slide() warned how many fit. A continued slide in a knitted deck has no title, and phw_add_slide() repeats the title, marked “(continued)” when the table has no caption. A table with no rows, such as one a filter left empty in a scheduled report, goes on one slide with its caption, header row and source, as in Word and HTML.
  • A table on a PowerPoint slide grows to fill the space it has. In a deck made with R Markdown or the Quarto phw-pptx format, a phw_flextable() with room to spare below ft.top now grows its text from 12 pt up to 18 pt, and its columns widen with it, never past the slide’s content area. Before, it stayed at 12 pt and a short table filled a small corner of the slide. phw_add_slide() grows a table up to 18 pt too, instead of 1.6 times its size, and now grows a phw_flextable() you pass in as well as a data frame; table_fit = FALSE keeps it at 12 pt. A table that continues on further slides grows only as far as it can without taking more slides, and shows the same size on each. A table that fits on one slide only with its row spacing squeezed below the 12 pt layout now continues on a second slide at a larger size.
  • A phw_flextable() in a deck made with R Markdown or Quarto is sized and split for the slides of that deck: those of its reference document, or of pandoc’s own deck when there is none. Before, tables were sized for the 13.33 x 7.5 in PHW deck, so in a 10 in wide deck, such as pandoc’s default one, columns ran off the right of the slide and rows off the bottom.
  • phw_add_slide() stops when given more content than the layout has room for, instead of silently using only the plot. It also refuses a chart or table on the navy Title Slide and Section Header layouts.
  • A group with an empty name ("") stops phw_colour_key() and the PHW colour scales. Give it a label, or make it NA to show it as missing.
  • phw_map() stops when every fill value is missing.
  • phw_spc() stops when a time point has more than one row, as when data holds several areas, and says to filter to one series or to draw one chart per series and combine them with phw_arrange(). Before, it pooled the series into one centre line and one set of limits, so a shift in one area could show as common cause variation.
  • phw_boundaries("community") returns every community as its own row, coded with its ONS code (W04...), with Welsh names in name_cy. Before, code was the community name, so communities that share a name, such as Castle in Cardiff and in Swansea, were merged into one area. Join your data by code, as names are not unique across Wales. Communities now come from the ONS Open Geography Portal (May 2026), in full, generalised and super generalised detail.
  • phw_epicurve() leaves unused factor levels out of the legend unless you give a colour key. Groups after an unused level take the next colour, so pass key to keep colours fixed across charts.
  • scale_*_phw_d(reverse = TRUE) now takes the first n colours of the palette and then reverses them, giving the same colours as phw_pal(n, reverse = TRUE). Reversed charts with fewer groups than the palette has colours change colour: with 3 groups, "main" gives #FF5D0C, #24A2B5, #285087 instead of #F43882, #FF5D0C, #24A2B5. "main" also carries on into "extended", so more than four groups no longer take colours from other palettes with a warning.
  • palette = "highlight" draws the first group in navy and every other group in light grey, however many groups there are. This applies to phw_pal(), scale_*_phw_d(), phw_colour_key(), phw_plotly() and the leaflet functions. With reverse = TRUE the last group is navy. Before, only the second group was grey and later groups took colours from other palettes, and phw_pal() stopped when asked for more than two.
  • scale_fill_phw_div() and scale_colour_phw_div() take midpoint in the units of the data, as ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2() does. With transform = "log10", midpoint = 1 now puts the neutral colour on 1, so a rate ratio chart shows values below and above 1 in different colours. Before, the midpoint was read on the log scale, so most charts came out in one colour. A midpoint the scale cannot show, such as the default 0 on a log scale, now stops with a message.
  • A sequential or diverging palette given to groups is spread over them, as phw_pal() does. This applies to scale_*_phw_d(), phw_map() with a text or factor fill, phw_epicurve(palette = ), phw_leaflet_palette(type = "factor"), phw_colour_key(), and the groups and traces of a plot_ly() chart in phw_plotly(). Traces that map no colour, from split = or separate add_trace() calls, leave out the near-white steps, which vanish on white. Before, groups took the first colours of the palette: three groups in "blues" were its three palest, "orange_navy" showed only its orange half, and ten deciles ran out of blues and took other PHW colours with a warning. Charts and maps of groups in these palettes change colour. A saved colour key keeps the colours it already gave its groups, and groups it gains later take the colours of the same palette furthest from the ones it already uses, so no two groups end up looking alike.
  • phw_leaflet_polygons() and phw_leaflet_palette(type = "factor") order groups as the PHW ggplot2 scales do: text sorted, factor levels in their order, with unused levels and NA left out. A group now has the same colour on a leaflet map as in a chart of the same data. Before, groups took colours in row order. phw_leaflet_palette() also no longer counts NA or unused levels when sizing the palette, which gave colours blended between PHW colours. Maps of groups that are not in sorted order change colour.
  • phw_leaflet_palette(type = "factor") gives each group its phw_colour_key() colour, as phw_leaflet_polygons() does: groups such as “Unknown” are grey, the other groups take the palette colours in turn, and more than twelve groups carry on with the warning the colour key gives instead of stopping. Before, “Unknown” took a palette colour and pushed the groups after it along by one.
  • phw_leaflet_palette(type = "factor") with no palette uses the default palette for groups, as phw_leaflet_polygons() and phw_colour_key() do, and follows options(phwstyle.palette = ). Before, it used "blues", so the first group was almost white. Numeric, binned and quantile palettes still default to "blues".
  • phw_leaflet_polygons(bins = ) reads bins as phw_map() does: the bins run from the lowest to the highest value, rounded out to tidy numbers, and are split at the breaks you give, or into that many classes for a single number. Before, an area below the first break or above the last was drawn grey as if it had no data and was left out of the legend, and bins = 5 gave 6 classes on a leaflet map and 3 in phw_map(). Binned leaflet maps change colour and legend.
  • phw_leaflet_polygons(bins = ) and phw_leaflet_palette(type = "bin") put an area in the same class, with the same colour, as phw_map() and scale_fill_phw_b(): a value on a break is in the class below it, and each class takes the shade the binned scale gives it. Before, a rate of exactly 5 with bins = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20) was in the first class on phw_map() and the second on the leaflet map, and the shades differed.
  • phw_map(bins = ) no longer draws an area grey as missing when a break lies outside the data, as in bins = c(0, 20, 100) for rates of 5 to 35.
  • phw_map(bins = ) and phw_leaflet_polygons(bins = ) with a single number draw that many classes of equal width with tidy edges, such as 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 for bins = 4 on rates of 12 to 88. Where no tidy width gives that number, they draw the nearest number they can and say so. Before, they drew fewer classes than asked for without a word: bins = 3 and bins = 4 both gave 2 classes on rates of 12 to 88.
  • phw_map(bins = 2) and phw_leaflet_polygons(bins = 2) split the areas into two classes at the tidy number nearest the median that leaves an area in each class. Before, they could draw every area in one colour, or put almost every area in one class when the data were skewed.
  • phw_map() checks bins as phw_leaflet_polygons() does: a single number below 2 stops with a clear error. Before, bins = 1 gave an error from another package and bins = 0 never returned.
  • phw_map(label = ) draws a label for every area, moving a label off a small area with a line to it where needed. Where labels still overlap at the size the map is drawn, a message names them and suggests saving the map larger or labelling fewer areas. Before, labels in crowded parts of the map, such as Caerphilly and Rhondda Cynon Taf, were left out without a word. To leave out labels that cannot be placed clear of the others, set options(ggrepel.max.overlaps = 10).
  • phw_plotly() colours the groups of a plot_ly() chart as the PHW ggplot2 scales do: unused levels are left out, NA is grey instead of invisible, groups such as “Unknown” are grey, and every group gets its own colour, with the warning phw_colour_key() gives when the palette runs out. Before, more than twelve groups or an unused level gave colours blended between PHW colours or shifted along by one. Pie slices take the colour of their group, not of their row, so a pie and a bar chart of the same data match. Traces added with their own data are coloured from that data, and all traces share one set of colours.
  • phw_plotly() gives a ggplot with no colour or fill scale of its own the colours the static chart has. Before, a continuous colour started from the palest blue, groups such as “Other” turned grey and NA was a lighter grey than in the static chart. Its groups take their colours from palette, as in a plot_ly() chart, and a group named in the palette, such as “Red” with palette = "rag", takes its own colour. Before, palette was ignored for a ggplot and its groups always had the default palette.
  • phw_plotly() gives a figure combined with plotly::subplot() the PHW colours. Before, it kept plotly’s default colours: groups, traces with no colour mapping and heatmaps all came out in plotly’s palettes. A group now has the same colour in every panel, and a trace that maps no colour, such as a Wales line, takes a palette colour no group uses, as in a single chart. If a panel sets its own colours, phw_plotly() keeps them and says how to give the other panels PHW colours.
  • phw_plotly() gives every panel of a figure combined with plotly::subplot(), or of a faceted ggplot, the PHW axis style. Before, only the first panel had it and the others kept plotly’s or ggplot2’s default axes.
  • phw_plotly() gives the groups of ggplots combined with plotly::subplot(), or converted with plotly::ggplotly(), the PHW colours, with a group the same colour in every panel. Before, they kept ggplot2’s default colours, even after use_phw_ggplot(), and a group could change colour from one panel to the next. A ggplot that sets its own colours with a scale keeps them.
  • phw_plotly() shades a ggplot coloured or filled by a number with the PHW blues when the ggplot was converted with plotly::ggplotly() or combined with plotly::subplot(), light for low values and navy for high ones, as in the static chart. Before, it kept ggplot2’s default gradient, which runs from dark to light, so the shading ran the other way.
  • phw_plotly() draws a missing group (NA) in grey in a figure combined with plotly::subplot(), as it does in a single chart. Before, its lines, bars and markers were invisible and its legend entry had no colour. This includes panels that set their own colors, such as phw_colour_key() or phw_pal().
  • phw_plotly() colours a figure combined with plotly::subplot() from its data when a colour column shares its name with an object or a function, such as class. Before, it stopped with an error, or warned that the palette had run out.
  • phw_plotly() shows the labels of phw_funnel() and phw_map(), and of any ggrepel::geom_text_repel() or ggrepel::geom_label_repel() layer, as plain text placed by its hjust and vjust. Before, plotly dropped them with a warning that this geom was not implemented.
  • phw_plotly() draws the 95% limits of phw_funnel() dashed and the 99.8% limits solid, as in the static chart. Before, plotly drew all four limit lines solid, so a reader could not tell the two limits apart.
  • phw_plotly() gives a label the same colour in every pie of a figure. Before, each pie took its colours from its own labels, so a label could be orange in one pie and teal in the next, and the shared legend showed the wrong colour for it.
  • phw_plotly() draws rows with a missing group in grey when the chart sets colors, either as a key such as phw_colour_key(...) or as a plain vector such as phw_pal(). Before, they were invisible: the legend showed “NA” with no line or markers. A key that gives "NA" its own colour keeps it.
  • phw_plotly() colours a plot_ly() chart by a number with the same blues as a ggplot2 chart, starting at #C9D3E1. This covers markers, lines, heatmaps, contours and choropleths, alone or combined with plotly::subplot(). Before, the scale started at the palest blue, so the lowest values almost vanished on white and the same data looked different in the two kinds of chart.
  • phw_plotly() draws a missing value in a plot_ly() chart coloured by a number in light grey, as the ggplot2 charts do. Before, plotly drew it near-black, so it read as the highest value.
  • phw_plotly() draws a missing heat map cell in light grey, as the static chart does, for geom_tile(), geom_raster() and plot_ly() heat maps. Before, the cell was left white, so it read as the lowest value.
  • phw_plotly() gives groups the PHW colours, and a number the PHW blues, when the chart starts with a trace that maps no colour, such as a Wales line added before the health boards. Before, plotly took the colours of all traces from the first one, so the groups kept plotly’s default colours and a number its default scale. A trace that maps no colour now takes a palette colour no group uses, so it never shares a colour with a group. A line added after the groups may change colour.
  • With palette = "rag" or "rag_accessible", groups called “Red”, “Amber” and “Green” (in any case) take the red, amber and green colours, whatever order they sort in. Before, they took the colours in sorted order, so Red was drawn green, Amber red and Green amber. The same holds for the named colours of "strategy" and for a named vector of colours, in every chart, map and table, with reverse = TRUE too. A colour key that had stored the wrong colour for such a group is corrected. Colours pinned with values or fixed still win.
  • The same name matching now applies to the default colours after use_phw_ggplot(palette = "rag"), so a chart with no colour scale of its own draws Red, Amber and Green in their own colours, as phw_plotly() does for the same chart. It also applies to phw_key_recolour(name, "rag") and phw_key_recolour(name, "strategy"). Before, both handed out colours in the groups’ sorted order.

Charts and maps

  • phw_pyramid(), phw_epicurve(), phw_map(), phw_funnel(), phw_spc() and phw_forest() stop when given a table() or a matrix and say what to pass instead. Before, they failed with “Can’t select within an unnamed vector” or “Column doesn’t exist”. For counts in a table(), pass as.data.frame(as.table(x)) with value = Freq to phw_pyramid(), count = Freq to phw_epicurve() or fill = Freq to phw_map().

  • A chart’s caption, such as the OS and ONS licence line of phw_map() or a phw_caption() source line, now wraps to the width the chart is drawn at by phw_save(), phw_finalise(), phw_add_slide() and the phw_*_document() formats. In a phw_arrange() figure, each plot’s caption wraps to the room under that plot. Captions are right-aligned, so before, a line wider than its room lost its start off the left edge or printed over the caption beside it: two maps side by side, or one map saved at half-page width, cut off their licence line.

  • A phw_arrange() figure moves its plots’ captions under the whole figure, each text once, when they do not fit under their plots: a map’s licence line beside a chart, or under two maps finished with phw_finalise(). They also move when the room the captions take makes maps so narrow that their titles run into each other. Before, the captions wrapped narrower on each try and the maps shrank with them: the figure collapsed into a strip with titles printed over each other, a map became a thumbnail with its licence line cut off at the left, or drawing stopped with the error “Viewport has zero dimension(s)”.

  • In a phw_arrange() figure, a plot’s title or subtitle wraps when it is wider than the room it has, up to the next title in its row or the right edge of the figure. Before, a map beside a chart with a legend of groups, such as phw_arrange(phw_epicurve(..., group = board), map), lost the end of the map’s title off the right edge, or printed it over the chart’s title when the map was on the left.

  • When a map makes a phw_arrange() figure narrower than the image, as it does stacked with ncol = 1, the legend collected under the figure wraps to the room from the figure’s left edge to the right edge of the image. Before, a legend of health boards ran off the right edge.

  • A legend of groups across the bottom or top of a chart takes more rows when one row is wider than the chart. Before, a legend of health boards at the default sizes stayed on one row and its last boards were cut off. This applies to charts saved with phw_save(), finished with phw_finalise(), arranged with phw_arrange(), placed with phw_add_slide() or drawn in a document made with the phw_*_document() formats. A legend given its own number of rows or columns, as in guide_legend(nrow = 1), keeps them.

  • theme_phw() puts each legend across the bottom or top of a chart on a row of its own, so a second legend no longer runs off the right edge. Before, the average line’s key in phw_epicurve(average = ) and the legends of a phw_arrange() figure that do not merge were placed beside the first legend and cut off. With phw_arrange(guides = "keep"), each plot’s legend now wraps to the width of that plot instead of the whole figure, so the legends no longer overprint each other.

  • The legend that phw_arrange() collects across the bottom or top of a figure starts at the left of the figure, under the title, and wraps to the figure’s width, as the legend of a single chart does with theme_phw(). Before, it started at the first chart’s y axis but wrapped to the whole figure width, so a legend of health boards at the default size ran off the right edge and its last board was cut off. Two legends of health boards, such as a line chart beside a bar chart, also took so many rows that the charts had no height left. With a theme that sets legend.location = "panel", the legend stays under the charts and wraps to their width.

  • A colour bar or colour steps legend across the bottom or top of a chart is long enough for its labels to be read. Before, it was about 2 cm long, so labels such as 600 to 1600 ran into each other and the first was cut off at the left edge. The bar is now at least twice as long, and longer when its labels need the room. This applies to scale_*_phw_c(), scale_*_phw_b() and scale_*_phw_div() wherever the chart is drawn, and to any colour bar in a chart saved with phw_save(), finished with phw_finalise(), arranged with phw_arrange(), placed with phw_add_slide() or drawn in a phw_*_document(). A bar on the right, as in phw_map(), and a bar given its own guide, keep their size.

  • phw_funnel() draws the same chart whatever the columns are called. Before, a denominator column named value was replaced by the computed percentage, so the points were drawn at the wrong place along the x-axis, and a label column named zone showed the zone names instead of the units. The added value and zone columns in $data now get a dot in front (.value, .zone) when data already has a column of that name.

  • phw_map() fills every part of an area when level is an sf data frame that holds the area as several rows, one per island or part, as some boundary files do. Before, only the first part took the area’s colour and the others were drawn grey, as areas with no data.

  • phw_map() follows the settings given to use_phw_ggplot(), such as base_size = 14 or accessible = TRUE, as the other ready-made charts do. Before, maps always used the theme_phw_map() defaults, so in a report set up for larger text they had smaller text than every other chart. Maps keep their legend on the right and have no gridlines.

  • The ready-made charts and maps, and the titles and source lines from phw_arrange(), phw_finalise() and phw_title_grob(), keep following the settings given to use_phw_ggplot() after a theme_update() or theme_replace(). Before, any such tweak sent them back to size 11 and accessible = FALSE without a word, while plain ggplots kept the settings. Setting a whole new theme, such as theme_set(theme_grey()), still sends them back to the defaults.

  • phw_arrange() no longer draws the legend of a plot that turned its own legend off with theme(legend.position = "none"). Before, collecting legends at legend turned it back on and drew it under the figure.

  • phw_arrange() draws the figure title, subtitle and source line with the settings given to use_phw_ggplot(), such as base_size = 16 or accessible = TRUE. Before, they kept the theme_phw() defaults, so the figure title could be smaller than the panel titles under it.

  • The source line added by phw_finalise() and the figure title from phw_title_grob() follow the settings given to use_phw_ggplot(), such as base_size = 16 or accessible = TRUE. Before, they were always 8.5 pt and 14 pt, so finalising an accessible chart made its source text smaller, and a figure title could be smaller than the panel titles under it. Give text_size or size to set the size yourself.

  • After use_phw_ggplot(), and so in every phw_*_document() format, groups from an ordered factor (from factor(..., ordered = TRUE), cut(..., ordered_result = TRUE) or lubridate::month(label = TRUE)) get the PHW palette, as unordered groups do. Before, they got ggplot2’s viridis colours. theme_phw() on its own still leaves them in viridis, because ggplot2 does not take their colours from the theme.

  • Ready-made charts check their data first. Text where numbers are needed, negative counts and impossible settings (funnel limits, targets, SPC baseline, pyramid left) stop with a message that says what to change. Epidemic curves say how many cases fall outside range.

  • phw_map() lists codes it could not match, and says when an area is drawn twice in one panel or when bins or key do not apply. phw_forest() says when a unit has more than one row in a panel. Faceting by period stays quiet in both.

  • Faceted phw_map() panels draw every area. An area with no data in a panel is drawn in the missing-value colour instead of being left out.

  • scale_shape_phw() and scale_linetype_phw() keep missing groups on the chart (new na.value). Past eight groups they stop with a clear message.

  • scale_fill_phw_d(na.translate = FALSE) and scale_colour_phw_d(na.translate = FALSE) leave missing groups off the chart, as ggplot2’s own scales do. Before, they were still drawn in grey, with no legend entry.

  • reverse = TRUE now works when the palette is a function, and a palette function gives groups its colours in its own order.

  • width and other bar settings passed through ... work in phw_epicurve() and phw_pyramid().

  • phw_pyramid() gives each sex the colour named after it in palette, as in palette = c(Female = "#24A2B5", Male = "#285087"). Before, it dropped the names and gave the colours out in the order of the sexes, so each sex could be drawn in the other’s colour. Its colours now come from scale_fill_phw_d(), so a sex value such as “Unknown” is drawn in grey, as in the other charts.

  • phw_pyramid(compare = ) stops when value is not given and compare has one row per age and sex, as a population table does, and says to count data and pass value. Before, each row of the population was counted as one person, so every outline was drawn the same size.

  • phw_pyramid() shows every level of the age factor, so an age band with nobody in it stays on the axis as a gap. Before, it was dropped when data had one row per person, or no row for that band.

  • phw_epicurve(average = ) repeats the average line in every panel when the chart is faceted by group. It is the total of all groups, so it belongs in each one. Before, it was drawn in the first group’s panel only, where it read as that group’s own average.

  • phw_epicurve(position = "dodge") draws each period’s bars inside the period, as stacked bars are, with the average line over their centre. Before, they were drawn half a period early.

  • phw_epicurve() labels the x axis at period starts, in a short format that suits interval: "6 Jan" for days and weeks, "Jan" for months and quarters and "2025" for years, with the year under the first label and wherever it changes. The first period is always labelled, so cases that all fall in one week or month still get a date. Labels that would overlap on a narrow chart are left out. Before, such a chart could have no date labels, and weekly labels fell on month starts rather than week starts.

  • theme_phw(), theme_phw_map(), phw_arrange(), phw_style_extensions() and the colour scales check their arguments when called, not when the plot is drawn.

  • phw_finalise() shows the organisation name when no logo is installed (change it with the new org), and stops with “file not found” for a missing logo file.

  • phw_finalise() keeps the footer readable on narrow charts. When the source does not fit beside the logo or organisation name, it moves above them and wraps to the width of the chart.

  • phw_finalise() on a map lays the footer out at the width of the map, which is often narrower than the image. The source stays beside the organisation name or logo, or moves above it, the whole footer stays on the image, and the map’s licence wraps as one paragraph. Before, at every default phw_save() size, the licence was printed over the organisation name, ran off the bottom of the image and left short lines such as “Open”.

  • phw_finalise() on a phw_arrange() figure keeps every panel, the figure title and the panel tags. Before, only the last panel was kept.

  • phw_finalise() on a phw_arrange() figure of maps, or of other plots that keep their shape, draws and saves. Before, printing or saving it failed with “‘respect’ must be logical or an ‘nrow’ by ‘ncol’ matrix”.

  • phw_finalise(note = ) with no source or date adds the note under the caption already on the plot. Before, the plot’s caption was dropped and only the note was shown.

  • phw_title_grob() makes room for a title or subtitle on more than one line. Before, the subtitle was drawn over the second title line, and without a subtitle the second line ran into the plot.

  • phw_save(bg = ) sets the background of the saved file, so bg = "transparent" gives a transparent PNG. Before, the white theme_phw() background covered it, and a phw_finalise() chart took bg only under its footer. With no bg, a chart keeps its own background as before.

  • phw_save() writes .eps and .ps files. Before, it failed with “family ‘Ubuntu’ not included in postscript() device”. Like .pdf, they use Ubuntu once it is installed with phw_install_fonts(). On macOS they need XQuartz, and without it phw_save() says so.

  • phw_number(big.mark = ) and phw_percent(big.mark = ) change the thousands separator, so phw_number(big.mark = "") labels years as 2024. Before, big.mark stopped with “matched by multiple actual arguments”.

Tables

  • In a Quarto document, the caption of phw_flextable() shows above the table in HTML, Word, PDF and Typst output, as it does in R Markdown. Before, Quarto dropped it without a word. A chunk that sets the tbl-cap option keeps Quarto’s caption instead.
  • phw_flextable() brings the Ubuntu web font into an HTML document, a Quarto HTML page and the RStudio Viewer, as phw_gt(), phw_reactable() and phw_datatable() do. Before, a computer without Ubuntu installed drew the table in a serif font unless another phwstyle output on the page loaded the font. htmltools::as.tags() on a phw_flextable() carries the font too.
  • Summary and group tables look the same in phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx(). Variable rows are shaded unless highlight = FALSE. phw_datatable() gains the spanner, two-level column headers, group separators and right-aligned statistics.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() keep labels held in row names, as as.data.frame() gives for a matrix or do.call(rbind, ...) for split data. They show as a first column with a blank header, as phw_reactable() already showed them. Before, the labels were dropped without a word, leaving numbers with no area names. Row names a column already holds, as data.frame(x = names(v), n = v) gives for a named tapply() or sapply() result, are not shown again, and phw_reactable() no longer shows them twice. Whole-number labels, such as the years, weeks or ages of a table() or tapply() result, show too, oldest or newest first. Row numbers are not labels and are not shown, including those rbind() keeps as text, such as "31", when filtered subsets share row numbers. Whole-number labels out of number order, such as rows sorted by a count, or sparse ones whose last few jump far above the rest, can look the same as those row numbers and are not shown: put them in a column instead.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable() and phw_write_xlsx() show a column whose name is missing, as a crosstab made with table(useNA = "ifany") or xtabs(addNA = TRUE) has, under the header “NA”, as phw_datatable() already did. Before, they failed with an error from another package. Rename the column to show another header.
  • phw_reactable() tables close with a navy rule and have a navy spanner.
  • phw_reactable() merges your columns into a summary table’s own column settings, so restyling one column keeps the indents, navy headings, alignment and blank missing values of the rest. A format in defaultColDef now applies to every column instead of being replaced by digits.
  • phw_reactable(group_col = ) and phw_flextable_groups() give each group the colour it has in a chart of the same data: the groups in use, sorted or in factor order. Before, colours followed the order of the rows, and an unused factor level took a colour. A colDef you give for the group column in columns now keeps the group colours.
  • phw_flextable_groups() leaves a row with a missing group uncoloured, as phw_reactable(group_col = ) does. Before, the row was given an NA colour and the table could not be saved to Word.
  • On a summary table such as one from phw_crosstab(), phw_flextable_groups() and phw_reactable(group_col = ) colour only the level rows. Before, the Total row took the next colour, so it read as one more group, and “Total” was added to the colour key. phw_reactable() also kept its own style for the label column and coloured no rows. The groups take the order of the table’s level rows, which is the factor order, as in a chart of the same data. Before, they were sorted as text, so age groups such as “5-14” and “15-44” got each other’s colours. In a table from phw_group_table(), each level keeps its colour when the first group has no rows for a level. Before, every level took the colour of the one before it.
  • phw_flextable_groups() and phw_reactable(group_col = ) can colour a table from phw_group_table(layout = "columns") by an outer column, such as the board in rows = c(board, sex). Each level row takes the colour of the group it sits under. Before, both stopped with a message about a group with an empty name.
  • phw_datatable() keeps the columnDefs you give in options for a summary table. Before, the table’s own column settings replaced them.
  • phw_datatable() accepts columns renamed with a named colnames, such as colnames = c(Cases = "cases"), and still rounds the numbers and styles a summary table’s renamed columns. Before, it stopped with an error from DT, or a summary table lost the styling of a renamed column.
  • phw_datatable() shows the names you give in colnames in the header of a summary table with a spanner or a multi-level header, such as a phw_crosstab(). An unnamed colnames now renames a summary table’s columns in order. Before, a spanner table kept its old names, and an unnamed colnames moved every name one column to the right.
  • phw_col_heat() shows whole-number columns, such as counts and totals, without decimals, and otherwise the digits of a summary table. Before, it showed every value with one decimal, as 61.0. phw_col_rag() takes the table as data. Given it, only the level rows of a summary table get a colour and a shape, and whole numbers show without decimals, as in phw_flextable_heat().
  • phw_reactable() and phw_datatable() show date-times at the clock time of their own time zone, as 2026-07-01 10:00:00, like phw_flextable(). Before, they showed them in UTC.
  • phw_write_xlsx() writes the spanner, navy labels, italic subtotals, a rule above the total, ISO dates and a bold right-aligned source. It checks x and accepts header_fill = "navy".
  • phw_write_xlsx(digits = 0) writes whole numbers as 1,235. Before, the number format had a trailing point, so Excel showed 1,235..
  • phw_write_xlsx() stops when two sheet names become the same once cleaned for Excel, such as "North/South" and "North?South", "Cases" and "cases", or two long names that share their first 31 characters. Before, the second table was written over the first sheet.
  • phw_write_xlsx() stops when the folder for file doesn’t exist, when file doesn’t end in .xlsx, and when title is neither one string nor one per sheet. Before, a missing folder gave an error from openxlsx2, a .xls name gave a file Excel complained about, and a short title was repeated, so a sheet could get another sheet’s title.
  • phw_flextable_heat(symbols = TRUE) keeps the table’s number format, so phw_flextable(digits = 1) shows “▼ 92.3”, not “▼ 92.34568”.
  • In a PDF report, the ▲ ■ ▼ shapes that phw_flextable_heat() adds to red, amber and green cells show as they do in HTML and Word. The Ubuntu font has no such shapes, so the PDF sets them in DejaVu Sans, or in Latin Modern Math when DejaVu Sans is not installed. Before, each shape was a missing-character box.
  • On a summary, cross-tab or group table, phw_flextable_heat() and phw_col_heat() colour only the level rows. Before, totals and subtotals were coloured too and set the top of the scale, so every other cell came out pale, and headings lost their grey band in the coloured columns. The total columns of a cross-tab or group table stay out of the scale too, so phw_flextable_heat(j = -1) no longer colours the Total column navy and every other cell near-white. Choose only total columns to colour them on a scale of their own.
  • With a fixed domain, phw_flextable_heat() and phw_col_heat() give a value beyond it the colour at the nearer end, as a chart does with oob = scales::squish. Before, the cell was left unfilled, so it read as no data, and scales gave a warning.
  • On a summary, cross-tab or group table, phw_flextable_bars() and phw_col_bar() draw bars on the level rows only, scaled to the largest level. Headings, subtotals and totals show the number only. Before, the grand total set the scale, so every level bar came out a sliver.
  • On a group table with totals = "subgroup", the “Total by …” block stays out of the heat and bar scales too, in phw_flextable_heat(), phw_flextable_bars(), phw_col_heat() and phw_col_bar(). Before, its rows set the top of the scale, so the group levels came out pale with short bars. The block looks the same as before.
  • phw_col_bar() and phw_col_heat() stop with a message when data is not a data frame, as phw_col_rag() does, and say how to convert a table() or a matrix. Before, a table() gave “Column Freq doesn’t exist”.
  • phw_flextable_heat() and phw_flextable_bars() choose j from the columns the table shows, so j = -1 or where(is.numeric) works on a table whose col_keys hides a column. Before, they stopped with an error from flextable about the hidden column.
  • Bars from phw_flextable_bars() show in a Word report made with phw_word_document(), as do links in a flextable. Before, Word called the file corrupt, and flextable’s warning was printed in the report. A flextable caption numbered with set_caption(autonum = ) now shows its number there too.
  • In phw_flextable(), the spanner above a summary, cross-tab or group table’s columns takes the same colour as the column labels below it. With style = "header" it is white on the navy band, with a white rule under it. Before, it was navy on navy and could not be read. It also follows accent and header_colour, and uses dark text with style = "light".
  • On a summary, cross-tab or group table with a spanner, phw_reactable() and phw_flextable() draw the navy top rule above the spanner and no navy rule inside the header, as do phw_gt(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx(). Before, phw_reactable() drew its top rule under the spanner, and phw_flextable() drew a short rule over the label column between the header rows.
  • phw_flextable(flextable_args = list(col_keys = )) can leave out or reorder the columns of a summary table, keeping the label columns first. Before, it failed inside flextable.
  • phw_flextable(col_labels = ) relabels the bottom header row of a group table with two or more column levels, as it does with one. Before, the labels were dropped without a message.
  • phw_gt() tables carry the bundled Ubuntu web font, dates are left-aligned and subtotals are italic.
  • phw_gt() and phw_gt_theme() tables in a Word document use the PHW font, with bold spanners and bold, shaded row groups. Before, Word showed them in Calibri. gt can’t make the column labels bold or indent the levels of a summary table in Word, so the first gt table knitted to Word in a session prints a note on the console suggesting phw_flextable(), the table renderer for Word. The note is for the author and is not written into the document.
  • phw_gt() left-aligns factor and logical columns, such as a health board stored as a factor or the label columns of a table() turned into a data frame, as the other table functions do. Before, gt centred them.
  • In a PDF report, the source line of a phw_gt() table now reads as it does in HTML: “Source:” and “Data correct as of” on separate lines, and characters such as & and % shown as typed. Before, the PDF showed a literal <br>, an & stopped the PDF from building and a % cut the line short.
  • phw_gt_theme(...) and phw_gt(theme_args = ) can change a setting phwstyle already sets, such as heading.align or data_row.padding. Your value replaces the PHW one. Before, these stopped with “matched by multiple actual arguments”.
  • phw_gt(gt_args = list(rowname_col = )) takes a summary, cross-tab or group table’s column name as it prints, such as "Characteristic", and a label column used as row names keeps its indents, bold headings and navy header. A name that is not a column stops with a message listing the columns. groupname_col stops with a message on these tables, because their label columns name a group on its first row only. Before, any column name failed inside gt with a list of columns the table does not show.
  • gt steps added after phw_gt() on a summary, cross-tab or group table, such as gt::cols_width(), gt::cols_label(), gt::cols_hide() or gt::fmt_number(), find its columns by the names the table shows, such as Characteristic or Total, as they do on a data frame. Before, they stopped with “Can’t select columns that don’t exist”.
  • phw_group_table(totals = "subgroup") heads the subgroup block with the variable label as you gave it, so “MRSA or MSSA (NHS lab)” is no longer printed as “mrsa or mssa (nhs lab)”. The new subgroup_label sets the heading, with {variable} for the label (default "Total by {variable}"), so all its words can be replaced, for example in Welsh. It no longer uses total_label.
  • phw_group_table(drop = FALSE) keeps factor levels that have no records, such as an empty age band or year, as rows and columns of zeros, as phw_crosstab() does. Before, it left them out.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() show NaN, Inf and -Inf as blank cells, as they show NA. Before, each showed them its own way, and phw_write_xlsx() wrote them as the Excel errors #VALUE! and #NUM!, so a SUM over the column failed.
  • phw_write_xlsx() writes a missing row label in a summary table as an empty cell, as the other renderers show it. Before, the cell held the text NA after the indent.
  • A phw_group_table() cell with no records is blank when fun gives no number for it, as max and mean do, and any NaN or Inf from fun is blank too. Counts and sums still show 0. Before, fun = max warned and showed -Inf.
  • phw_group_table(layout = "columns") with three or more row variables puts the levels of the subgroup block (“Total by …”) in the innermost variable’s column. Before, they sat in the second column.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() show a phw_group_table() with the decimal places set by its digits, unless you give them their own digits. Before, digits was ignored without percent, so fun = mean values showed with one decimal place.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() show a year column without a thousands separator, as 2021, not 2,021. A year column holds whole numbers from 1800 to 2200 and has the word “year”, “yr” or “blwyddyn” in its name, such as Year, year_of_onset or Blwyddyn. Other numbers keep their separator.
  • phw_summary_table() shows a blank, not “( to )”, when a statistic can’t be calculated, and labels can be a named character vector.
  • phw_summary_table() summarises a difftime column, such as a length of stay made by subtracting two dates, as a number in its own units: one median (IQR) or mean (SD) row. Before, each value became its own row.
  • phw_summary_table() summarises a date or date-time column, such as an onset date, as one median (IQR) or mean (SD) row shown as dates (dd/mm/yyyy). Before, each date became its own row, so a line list with a date column gave a table of hundreds of rows.
  • Filtering the rows of a summary, cross-tab or group table, or selecting some of its columns, with [, head(), subset() or dplyr’s filter(), slice(), arrange() and select(), keeps the bold headings, indents, rules and column headers on the rows and columns kept. Before, every renderer styled the wrong rows or stopped with an error. A table without its label columns becomes a plain data frame. A table whose rows no longer match its styling, for example after rbind(), stops with a message suggesting as.data.frame().
  • A column added to a summary, cross-tab or group table, with dplyr’s mutate() or with $<-, shows in every renderer with an empty cell above it. Before, mutate() and every renderer failed with “subscript out of bounds” on a table with column levels, and on a table with one spanner the new column sat under the spanner. Spanners and column levels follow their columns when they are moved or renamed.
  • phw_rate_table() stops with a message naming the column when the count or population column is text, instead of failing inside sum().
  • Table and column helpers give clear errors for duplicated column names, negative bar values, a data frame where a flextable is needed, or an unknown style.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() stop when given a table() or a matrix and suggest converting it with as.data.frame(). Before, flextable and reactable failed with “subscript out of bounds” and phw_gt() drew an empty table. phw_datatable(), which converted them itself, now stops the same way.
  • phw_as_summary(), phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab() and phw_group_table() stop when given a table() or a matrix and say what to pass instead. Before, phw_as_summary() dropped the row names, phw_summary_table() counted the cells as records, and phw_crosstab() and phw_group_table() failed with “Can’t select within an unnamed vector”. For counts you already have, phw_crosstab() takes as.data.frame(as.table(x)) with count = Freq, and phw_group_table() takes it with value = Freq.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() leave out the geometry of an sf data frame, such as phw_boundaries() joined to case counts, and show the other columns. Before, the geometry showed as a column of coordinates, “[[XY]]” or “[object Object]”, and in Excel it ran past the cell size limit. phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab(), phw_group_table() and phw_as_summary() also leave it out, so an sf line list or area table is summarised by its other columns. Before, areas stopped with an error from the units package, and points added a “geometry” variable with one row per point.
  • phw_flextable(), phw_gt(), phw_reactable(), phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() show a difftime column, such as a length of stay made by subtracting two dates, as a plain number in its own units. It is right-aligned like other numbers, and a missing value is blank. Before, flextable showed “4 days”, gt centred the column and reactable showed a missing stay as “NA”. Name the unit in the column heading, for example “Length of stay (days)”.
  • phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab() and phw_group_table() keep the label attributes of columns when rows are left out for a missing value. Before, the headings fell back to the column names.

Slides and documents

  • The PowerPoint template from phw_reference_pptx(), used by phw_pptx() and the Quarto phw-pptx format, now has Comparison and Content with Caption layouts. pandoc uses these for a slide with text followed by a chart, and for two columns that hold text and a chart. Before, those slides fell back to pandoc’s own plain layout, with a small unstyled title.
  • The date from a deck’s YAML header is now light on the navy title slide of the PowerPoint template from phw_reference_pptx(), like the subtitle. Before, it was grey on navy and hard to read. A footer or slide number on the title slide or a Section Header slide is light too.
  • A grey PNG logo with transparency now works like a colour one in phw_finalise(), phw_word_document(), phw_pdf_document(), phw_latex_header(), phw_reference_docx() and use_phw_quarto(). Before, it stopped with “a raster array must have exactly 3 or 4 planes”.
  • In the Quarto phw-docx format, a captioned figure shows in full, with its source line. Before, the right edge of each chart was cut off, and navy rules were drawn above and below it. Charts are now drawn 6.3 by 3.9 inches by default, as in phw_word_document(). Quarto lays out a captioned figure or table in a Word table, which now has the Layout Table style from phw_reference_docx(), with no rules or cell padding. With Quarto 1.5, whose pandoc cannot style that table, a figure or table on its own is taken out of it instead. Run use_phw_quarto(template = "none", overwrite = TRUE) to update the extension in an existing project.
  • phw_reference_docx() writes a document with no text in it. A Word file made with officer::read_docx(phw_reference_docx()) now starts with your own content. Before, it started with a page of sample text from pandoc.
  • phw_add_slide() places content on every layout. Two Content fills the left side first, and Title Only and Blank place the chart, table or text in the free space.
  • phw_add_slide() puts content into a layout’s content placeholders and leaves text-only ones empty, so on a template’s Comparison layout the chart and table fill the left and right areas. Before, the first went into the small heading above the left area.
  • phw_add_slide() checks its arguments before it adds a slide, so a call that stops leaves the deck unchanged. It accepts a phw_finalise() chart as a picture.
  • phw_add_slide(table_fit = TRUE) no longer grows a table that fits the slide until it runs off the bottom. Before, tables of about 10 to 12 rows grew past the content area, and the warning asked you to split them. A cell with more than one line now counts as that many lines when the table is sized.
  • phw_add_slide(table_fit = TRUE) no longer narrows the columns of a table that is wider than the content area until numbers and labels break across lines. Its headings wrap first, then its cells, at no less than 12 points. A table still too wide gives a warning that names how many columns it has.
  • phw_add_slide() scales the text of a phw_arrange() figure as one: every panel, the figure title and the source line. Before, only the last panel was scaled.
  • phw_add_slide() wraps a chart’s caption to fit the slide when its enlarged lines are too wide. Before, the start of each line was cut off, so a phw_map() on a half-width slide lost the start of its OS and ONS licence line.
  • A flextable’s caption, such as “Table 1 …” from phw_flextable(), now shows on a phw_add_slide() slide, in a row at the top of the table. Before, PowerPoint left it out without a word.
  • A phw_flextable() caption now shows above the table when the table is knitted into a PowerPoint deck, from R Markdown powerpoint_presentation() or the Quarto phw-pptx format. Before, the slide kept the table and its source line but dropped the caption.
  • In a PDF document, a phw_flextable() caption reads as it does in Word and HTML: “Table 1 Counts by board”, or no number when you give none. Before, LaTeX added its own label, giving “Table 1. Table 1 Counts by board”.
  • In a Word document, a phw_gt() caption reads as it does in HTML and PDF: “Table 2 Cases by area”, or no number when you give none. Before, gt added its own number, giving “Table 1: Table 2 Cases by area”.
  • In a Word or PDF document, a phw_flextable() table wider than the page now fits the text width. Its headings wrap first, then its cells, and its text shrinks to no less than 8 pt if the words alone are still too wide. A table that cannot fit even then gives a warning. Before, a summary table or cross-tab by the seven health boards ran past the right margin and lost its last columns.
  • In a PowerPoint deck made with R Markdown or Quarto, a phw_flextable() table wider than the slide now fits the slide’s content area, in the same way, except that its text stays at 12 pt or larger. A table that cannot fit gives a warning. Before, a summary table by the seven health boards ran off the right edge of the slide and lost its last columns without a warning.
  • In a PDF document, a phw_gt() table stays where it is in the text, a table longer than the page carries on over the next pages with its title and column labels repeated, and a table wider than the text shrinks to fit it. Before, LaTeX moved the table, often to the next page after the paragraph that follows it, a table longer than the page ran over the footer and lost its last rows and source line, and a summary table by health board ran past the right margin and lost its Total column.
  • In phw_pdf_document(), and in other LaTeX formats that use phw_latex_header(), a captioned chart stays where it is in the text, under its heading, as in Word and HTML. Before, LaTeX could move it past later sections, so a section had no chart and the chart appeared under another heading. Set the chunk option fig.pos to place a chart yourself.
  • On the title slide and section header of your own template, phw_add_slide() gives text the template’s colour and size, and the source line is white only when the slide background is dark. Before, both were near-white on every such slide, so they vanished on a white one.
  • The title and text on a title slide or section header are in the PHW font, the title is bold, and title_size applies when you give it. Before, both used the template’s font and size and the title was not bold.
  • Captions leave out a missing or empty source, date or note instead of printing “NA”, and name a misspelt caption argument. A caption_args list without names stops with a message that asks for a named list.
  • The R Markdown formats add your own css, includes and pandoc_args to the PHW ones, and LaTeX characters in team print as typed.
  • phw_latex_header(file) writes the page band image beside file, as <name>-band.png, and points the header at it. Before, the header pointed at a temporary image that was gone in the next R session, so a saved header stopped the PDF build with “File not found”.
  • In phw_pdf_document(), a document whose sections are ## headings, as in the R Markdown file RStudio creates, is numbered 1, 2, 3, and its sections look like top-level sections. Before, they were numbered 0.1, 0.2, 0.3. The top heading level a document uses is numbered from 1.
  • phw_pdf_document() keeps the dev you give it instead of always using "ragg_png".
  • phw_pdf_document() uses fontsize, documentclass, geometry and colorlinks from the YAML header or from pandoc_args in place of the PHW ones. Before, the PHW values silently won, and a fontsize in pandoc_args gave LaTeX an option it doesn’t know, so the text was 10pt. A geometry that sets only the margins keeps A4 pages: set papersize to change the paper. The Quarto phw-pdf format works the same way.
  • phw_pdf_document() and the Quarto phw-pdf format colour links in PHW colours: web links in PHW blue, as in Word and HTML, and cross-references in navy. Before, pandoc’s own blue and maroon replaced them. Set linkcolor, urlcolor, citecolor or filecolor in the YAML header to change them.
  • phw_pdf_document() and the Quarto phw-pdf format build a document with two or more authors, and the cover lists each author on its own line. Before, LaTeX failed to compile and no PDF was written.
  • phw_download_logos() saves nothing when the reply isn’t an SVG.
  • A logo folder with only PNG logos now shows the logo in phw_html_document(), phw_header(), phw_page_navbar() and the Quarto dashboard, slide and Typst formats. Before, they showed the organisation name or nothing, and phw_has_logo() returned FALSE. phw_has_logo() is now TRUE whenever the white PNG logo is available.

Interactive outputs and colours

  • phw_plotly() spaces the legend of a ggplot correctly in Chrome, Edge and the RStudio and Positron Viewer. Before, on a computer without the Ubuntu font installed, each label ran into the next item and the last label was cut off, as in “4-week averag” on an epidemic curve. The legend, axis titles, tick labels and facet strips now fall back to Arial while the Ubuntu font loads, as a plot_ly() chart already did. This holds for a chart made with plotly::ggplotly() and for a plotly::subplot() of ggplots too.
  • phw_plotly() draws an empty chart for a ggplot whose data a filter left with no rows, as plotly::ggplotly() does, so a scheduled report still knits in a week where nothing matched. Before, it stopped with the error “values must be length 1”. The same holds for a layer with no rows next to layers with data, and for a chart made with plotly::ggplotly().
  • phw_plotly() also draws the empty chart, with its title, axis titles and source, for a line, step, error bar, boxplot or point range layer with no rows, alone or next to layers with data. Before, plotly stopped with errors such as “argument 1 is not a vector” or “‘by’ must specify a uniquely valid column”.
  • phw_reactable() and phw_plotly() now bring the Ubuntu web font into the page, as phw_datatable() and phw_leaflet() do. Before, a table without a caption and every chart fell back to Arial.
  • Leaflet maps draw areas with a missing value in the house grey, matching the legend, and give one clear message when a numeric fill has no values to colour by.
  • phw_plotly() colours traces that map color with the PHW palette, gives heatmaps and contours the PHW sequential scale, and keeps your own annotations.
  • phw_plotly() keeps the chart title and axis titles of a plot_ly() chart, whether set with layout() or taken from the columns, and styles them in the PHW font and colours. Before, it removed them. A chart with one trace no longer gets a legend reading “trace 0”: legend now sets where a legend goes, and only legend = "none" decides whether there is one.
  • phw_plotly() with the legend at the bottom places the legend under the axis title and the source line under the legend, however many rows the legend wraps to and whatever the chart’s size. Before, a legend of seven health boards ran under the source line, and on a short chart it sat on the axis title. Other annotations, including the axis titles of a faceted ggplot, stay where they are. A bottom margin you set with margin = list(b = ) is kept as the least space under the chart.
  • phw_plotly(legend = "right") puts the legend of a ggplot to the right of the plot, as it does for a plot_ly() chart. Before, a chart with theme_phw() kept its legend under the chart, as a vertical list next to the source line.
  • phw_plotly() names the legend of a ggplot the way the static chart does, with one entry per group. Before, a chart with a second layer in the legend, such as phw_epicurve(average = ) or phw_forest(target = ), read “(A,1)” and “(3-week average,1)”, and the forest plot listed each group twice.
  • phw_plotly() keeps a legend title set with plotly::layout(), and the legend title a ggplot or phw_map() shows. Before, it removed every legend title. A ggplot whose theme hides the legend title, as theme_phw() does, still has none.
  • phw_plotly() keeps a ggplot’s subtitle, under the title, and its caption, as the source line under the chart. Before, both were dropped, so a chart captioned with labs(caption = phw_caption(...)) lost its source. A source or date you pass still replaces the caption.
  • phw_plotly() makes room above the plot for every line of the title and subtitle and for the facet strips of a ggplot. Before, the strips were drawn over the subtitle, and a subtitle on more than one line ran into the plot.
  • phw_plotly() shows each bar of phw_pyramid() on hover by its sex, age band and value, formatted as on the axis: “Female, 0-4: 240,000” or “Female, 0-4: 25.5%”. Before, the left-hand sex read as a negative, unrounded number such as “x: -240000”. A ggplot that maps the text aesthetic now shows only that text on hover, as plotly::ggplotly(tooltip = "text") does.
  • phw_plotly() gives a chart converted with plotly::ggplotly() first the same legend names and hover as the ggplot itself. Before, phw_plotly(plotly::ggplotly(g)) read “(Cardiff,1)” and “(Target,1)” in the legend, and the hover of phw_pyramid() showed the left-hand sex as negative values.
  • phw_plotly() gives ggplots combined with plotly::subplot() the same legend names as each chart on its own. Before, a panel with an average or target line, such as phw_epicurve(average = ), read “(Cardiff,1)” and “(4-week average,1)”. A group now also keeps one colour across the panels when a line maps a colour of its own next to filled bars. Before, the first group could be navy in one panel and pink in the next.
  • phw_plotly() draws the secondary axis of a ggplot, such as one from phw_sec_axis(), on the right (or the top) with its own breaks and title, and it stays with its own chart in a plotly::subplot() figure passed to phw_plotly(). Before, the axis was dropped without a word, so the second measure was read against the main axis: a positivity of 30% read as 184 cases. Hover still shows the second measure in the units of the main axis; map the text aesthetic to show it in its own. A faceted chart can’t show the axis and now warns.
  • phw_leaflet_polygons(), phw_boundaries(), phw_plotly() and the colour key functions check their input first. phw_boundaries() checks crs before downloading anything.
  • phw_key_recolour() carries "main" on into "extended" past four groups, as phw_colour_key() does. It keeps the colour of neutral groups such as “Other”, including one set with neutral_colour. Its new neutral argument names which groups those are.
  • Pointing phw_key_file() at another file, or at NULL, forgets the keys read from the old file. Before, a second report rendered in the same session used the first report’s colours and saved them into its own key file. Keys made before any key file was set are kept.
  • phw_key_set() changes the accessible copy of a key (name@accessible) too, when there is one. Before, once a key file held that copy from an earlier accessible render, a colour set by hand reached only the default version of the report. Colours go into the copy as they do when it is first made: a default-palette colour that isn’t in "accessible" keeps the group’s accessible colour, or takes the next free one.
  • phw_plotly_colorscale() and phw_pal() take a whole number for n. Before, phw_plotly_colorscale(n = 2.5) made a scale whose last stop was 0.67, not 1.
  • phw_contrast(), phw_text_on() and phw_cvd() return NA for a missing colour instead of treating it as white, and accept palette names.
  • show_phw_palettes() picks each swatch’s label colour with phw_text_on(), so mid-tone swatches such as teal, orange and pink get dark labels, which contrast more than white.
  • phw_page_navbar(header_args = ) overrides the title and subtitle by name, so the logo link keeps its address.
  • phw_bs_theme() takes Bootstrap version 4 or 5 only.
  • phw_header() brings its own styles, so the gradient band, white logo and Ubuntu titles show on any page. Before, they showed only on a page themed with phw_bs_theme(), and elsewhere the white logo was invisible.

Documentation

  • The gallery, the demo script and the website articles use larger made-up data: line lists in the thousands, weekly and monthly series over several years, 22 areas, 5-year age bands and maps of every local authority or MSOA. The charts now look as they do on real outputs. Help-page examples and the package vignette stay small.

Requirements

  • PowerPoint slides need officer 0.6.7 or later (was 0.6.6). phw_add_slide() places content in the layout’s own placeholders, which needs officer::ph_location_id(). With officer 0.6.6 it stopped with “‘ph_location_id’ is not an exported object”.

phwstyle 0.3.0

New charts and maps

  • phw_forest() draws your own estimates and intervals by unit, sorted by value. With target, a dashed line marks the target and units are coloured and shaped Higher, Similar or Lower. It calculates nothing.
  • phw_map() joins your data to Welsh boundaries by area code and returns a styled choropleth for Word and PDF. Fills can be continuous, binned or by group, areas with no data are grey, and the boundary attribution is the default caption. It works with facet_wrap(). Area labels are moved apart when ggrepel is installed.
  • phw_epicurve() gains average and average_label, which draw a trailing average of the total count as a black line with its own legend entry. $data gains an average column. Its default date labels now stay within the data, so the last label is no longer cut off.
  • phw_funnel() and phw_spc() gain labels, a named vector that renames zones or signals, and pass ... to their points.

Tables

  • phw_as_summary() gives a table you built yourself, for example with dplyr, the bold variable rows, indented levels and total rows of the built-in summary tables in every renderer.
  • phw_datatable() now styles summary tables like phw_reactable(): bold variable, subtotal and total rows, indented levels, and no paging or sorting by default.
  • phw_reactable() rounds numbers like the other renderers: whole-number columns show no decimals and other numbers show digits (default 1), with thousands separators.

Slides

  • phw_pptx() opens a bundled 16:9 PHW template with Ubuntu text and navy titles. phw_reference_pptx() writes it to a file, like phw_reference_docx().
  • phw_add_slide() gains alt, the screen-reader text for the chart or table, and caption_args. It takes the slide master from the layout, so your own templates work.
  • phw_add_slide() makes charts and tables readable on a slide. Chart text is enlarged 1.5 times (plot_scale), and tables built from a data frame or summary grow to fill the content area (table_fit). A tall table tightens its row spacing so the text can still grow.
  • The Quarto extension gains a phw-pptx format.

phwstyle 0.2.0

Tidyverse-style column arguments

  • Functions that take columns now take them the way dplyr does: unquoted names, c(a, b) for several, and helpers such as starts_with(). For example phw_epicurve(cases, onset, group = organism) and phw_group_table(dat, rows = c(group, type), cols = year). They work in a pipe after dplyr verbs, and accept tibbles. This covers phw_epicurve(), phw_pyramid(), phw_funnel(), phw_spc(), phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab(), phw_rate_table(), phw_risk_table(), phw_group_table(), phw_flextable_heat(), phw_flextable_groups(), phw_flextable_bars(), phw_reactable(group_col = ), phw_col_bar(), phw_col_heat() and phw_leaflet_polygons().
  • Code that passes column names as strings keeps working, including names held in a variable.
  • phw_leaflet_polygons() labels and popups can be built from columns, e.g. label = paste(name, rate).
  • phwstyle now imports tidyselect. The examples, vignettes and starter documents are written with dplyr and tidyr.

Requirements

  • phwstyle now needs R 4.3 or later (was 4.1). R 4.3 is the oldest version for which Windows users can install, without compiling, versions of ggplot2, flextable, rmarkdown and the other packages phwstyle works with.
  • DESCRIPTION states the oldest version of each optional package that phwstyle works with.

New palettes

  • "extended" now has twelve colours instead of eight: the four "main" colours; then black, green and gold from the NHS Wales logo guidelines and the phw.nhs.wales website; then mint and bright green from the Long-Term Strategy; then a blue, a dark green and a violet chosen to stay distinct from the rest. Every pair stays apart for colour-blind readers. Charts with five or more groups change colour: the fifth to eighth colours were gold, purple, green and grey.
  • "strategy": the colours of the six strategic priorities in the Long-Term Strategy 2023 to 2035, for work reported by priority.
  • "greens": a sequential green palette, from a pale tint to the website green, for scale_*_phw_c(), scale_*_phw_b(), heat tables, maps and plotly colour scales.
  • New colours in phw_colours: mint and green_bright.

Changes to default colours

  • The default palette no longer switches to "accessible" above four groups. Charts with more than four groups now carry on from "main" into "extended" (navy, teal, orange, pink, then black, green, gold and more), so every chart in a report starts with the same colours however many groups it has. Before, a five-group chart was drawn in the accessible palette next to four-group charts in the main one. This applies everywhere groups are coloured: ggplot2 defaults, scale_*_phw_d(), phw_epicurve(), phw_colour_key(), phw_pal(), phw_plotly(), phw_reactable(), phw_flextable_groups() and phw_leaflet_polygons(). Charts with five or more groups that relied on the old switch will change colour. To keep the colour-blind safe palette, switch it on (next item).
  • Accessible colours are now a switch. Turn it on once and every chart, table and widget uses the "accessible" palette, for any number of groups, so one document can be rendered both ways:
    • R Markdown: new palette argument for phw_html_document(), phw_word_document() and phw_pdf_document(), e.g. rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_options = list(palette = "accessible")). The palette is put back when the render finishes.
    • Quarto: phw-palette: accessible in the document’s YAML header.
    • Any route: the environment variable PHWSTYLE_PALETTE=accessible, for switching one render from the command line.
    • use_phw_ggplot(palette = "accessible") and options(phwstyle.palette = "accessible") work as before.
    theme_phw(accessible = TRUE) (larger text, thicker lines) is separate and unchanged: it doesn’t change colours, and the palette switch doesn’t change sizes. See ?phw_default_palette.
  • Colour keys keep a separate copy for the accessible palette, stored as name@accessible with the groups in the same order, so a keyed chart follows the switch and both versions of a report keep their colours between runs. A key used with palette = "accessible" before this version is carried over. phw_key_reset() clears both copies.
  • use_phw_ggplot() now gives the same result on ggplot2 3.5 and 4.0. A layer with no colour of its own (geom_col(), geom_line(), geom_point()…) is navy on both; before, it was navy on 3.5 but grey or near-black on 4.0. Text, reference lines (geom_hline() and friends) and box plot outlines use the PHW text colour, and box plots and violins keep a white fill. Line widths, point sizes and text sizes now match too, so accessible = TRUE thickens lines on ggplot2 3.5 as well.
  • A plot left on the default colours now gets exactly the colours scale_*_phw_d() would give the same number of groups. Past the end of a palette that means spare colours from the other PHW palettes and a warning, instead of blended in-between colours.

Boundaries

  • phw_boundaries("msoa") and phw_boundaries("lsoa") work again. The ONS Open Geography Portal stopped publishing the layers they used, so both now come from DataMapWales (Welsh Government), with the super generalised ONS boundaries as the alternative. MSOAs from DataMapWales have no Welsh names, so name_cy is missing for them.
  • Where a geography is published by more than one source, phw_boundaries() tries the others if the first cannot be reached, and warns which boundaries it returned.
  • An area that a source holds as several rows, such as an LSOA with islands, is returned as one row.
  • phw_boundaries() keeps working when a publisher replaces or withdraws a layer after phwstyle was installed. If none of the layers it lists can be downloaded, it fetches the current list of layers from the phwstyle repository and tries those, and failing that returns boundaries saved from an earlier release, with a warning in both cases. Set options(phwstyle.boundary_update = FALSE) to stop it fetching the list.
  • The list of layers is now checked every week instead of every month. A layer is listed only once a test download works, and a new ONS release is used once its generalised boundaries are published, so the default level of detail is never lost while a release is part way out.

Fixes for older versions of other packages

  • use_phw_ggplot(), and so every phw_*_document() R Markdown format, no longer fails with “Can’t find geom called”histogram”” on ggplot2 older than 4.0. The geom defaults are now set one by one, so a geom that an installed ggplot2 doesn’t have is skipped.
  • On ggplot2 older than 4.0, a plot that mapped a variable to colour or fill and had no scale of its own failed with “argument”n” is missing” after use_phw_ggplot(), which meant most charts in a phw_*_document(). The default scales are now set up correctly there, and continuous and binned defaults use the same blues as on ggplot2 4.0.
  • The R Markdown formats no longer stop a whole render if styling the charts or the flextables fails. The document is rendered and a warning says what was left unstyled and why.
  • phw_gt() works with gt older than 0.11.1, which doesn’t export all_of().
  • phw_page_navbar() works with bslib older than 0.9.0, which has no navbar_options().
  • phw_write_xlsx() no longer fails with “Failed to save workbook” on computers where R names a zip program that isn’t installed.
  • The Quarto phw-typst format works with Quarto 1.5 and 1.6. It failed there with “unexpected argument: spacing”, and top-level headings came out numbered “0.1” and too small.
  • phw_pdf_document() no longer fails on a document with a flextable when the Ubuntu font is not installed on the computer. Tables now use the bundled font, as the rest of the document does.

Other changes

  • The ready-made charts (phw_epicurve(), phw_pyramid(), phw_funnel(), phw_spc()) follow the settings given to use_phw_ggplot(), such as base_size = 14 or accessible = TRUE. Before, they always used the theme_phw() defaults.
  • vignette("phwstyle") has a new section, “How the pieces fit together”: what each function switches on, what you still need to add to a plot after setup, and how your own scales and theme settings take priority.
  • New phw_sec_axis() draws a second measure against its own axis, on linear and log scales, without working out the rescaling by hand. theme_phw() spaces the titles of top and right axes like the bottom and left ones.

phwstyle 0.1.2

  • Resubmission to CRAN. The phw_datatable() example no longer opens a browser when examples are run non-interactively.

phwstyle 0.1.1

  • First CRAN submission. Fixes the notes from the automated CRAN checks on 0.1.0 (wording in DESCRIPTION and links in the README).

phwstyle 0.1.0

  • First release.
  • Brand colours and palettes (phw_colours, phw_pal()), with WCAG contrast helpers. Every palette argument also takes your own colours.
  • A colour-blind safe accessible palette, phw_cvd(), phw_check_colours(), scale_shape_phw() and scale_linetype_phw().
  • Colour keys that keep each group’s colour across charts and reports (phw_colour_key(), scale_*_phw_d(key = ), phw_key_file()).
  • Extension geoms styled automatically (phw_style_extensions()), and multi-plot figures with phw_arrange() and phw_title_grob(). phw_finalise() accepts patchworks and grobs.
  • Summary tables for reports and epidemiology (phw_summary_table(), phw_crosstab(), phw_rate_table(), phw_risk_table(), phw_group_table() for nested row and column groups with group, subgroup and table totals), rendered by phw_flextable() and phw_reactable(), plus column formats (phw_flextable_bars(), phw_col_bar(), phw_col_heat(), phw_col_rag()).
  • phw_plotly() styles every plotly chart type; phw_plotly_colorscale().
  • Public health charts: phw_epicurve(), phw_pyramid(), phw_funnel() and phw_spc().
  • More outputs: gt (phw_gt(), phw_gt_theme()), gtsummary (use_phw_gtsummary()), DT (phw_datatable()), leaflet (phw_leaflet(), phw_leaflet_polygons(), phw_leaflet_palette()), Excel (phw_write_xlsx()) and PowerPoint (phw_pptx(), phw_add_slide()).
  • phw_boundaries() downloads and caches boundaries for 13 Welsh geographies from the ONS Open Geography Portal and DataMapWales, including health boards and GP clusters; phw_boundary_levels() lists them.
  • phw_setup_check() lists missing fonts, packages and tools and offers to install them.
  • Bundled Ubuntu font with Arial fallback (phw_font(), phw_install_fonts()).
  • ggplot2 theme and scales (theme_phw(), theme_phw_map(), scale_*_phw_*(), use_phw_ggplot(), phw_finalise(), phw_save()).
  • Tables and widgets: phw_flextable(), phw_flextable_heat(), phw_reactable(), phw_plotly().
  • Shiny: phw_bs_theme(), phw_header(), phw_page_navbar().
  • R Markdown formats: phw_html_document(), phw_word_document(), phw_pdf_document().
  • Quarto extension with HTML, Word, Typst, LaTeX PDF, revealjs and dashboard formats (use_phw_quarto()).
  • Captions and dates (phw_caption(), phw_date()), with every word changeable.
